newsitem.title: USA: Space station schedule hit by Russian module delays.
newsitem.headline: Space station schedule hit by Russian module delays.

text.p: The United States-led international space station programme faces major disruption because a crucial Russian module will not be launched on time, according to NASA documents obtained by Reuters.
Construction of the Service Module, part of Russia's contribution to the project, is running at least eight months late, an internal NASA status report said.
A team of senior NASA space station managers who visited Moscow in late November learned the launch of the Service Module had slipped to December 31, 1998 from April 20 of that year.

The delayed launch date itself is dependent on Russian funding for the module becoming available before the middle of this month. But that funding has failed to materialise so far, meaning that the December 1998 date could slip further.

"The financial problems ... are bigger than we thought," the document said. R.K. Energia, the Russian company managing the project, owes "close to $100 million" to its subcontractors and most of them will not accept any new work until those debts had been paid, the document said.
The funding problems may not be resolved until U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin meet in February.

The delay has thrown NASA's space station assembly schedule into disarray because assembly of the outpost cannot proceed without the crucial module. Space agency managers were scrambling to minimise the impact of the delay, including dusting off plans for a U.S.-built alternative.
The Service Module, the nerve centre of the space station, was to be the third major component of the sprawling outpost.

The 46,300-pound (20,577 kilograms) component was to serve as a control post and living quarters for the first space station crew, who were due to arrive in May 1998 to oversee the construction effort.

Construction of the $30 billion station was due to begin in less than a year's time with the launch of a Russian-built, U.S.-financed, propulsion and power module in November 1997. The construction of that spacecraft has so far remained more or less on schedule.

It will take 27 shuttle flights and 44 Russian launches between 1997 and 2002 to assemble and operate the station. Once completed the complex will stretch 356 feet (119 meters) from end-to-end, weigh 940,000 lbs (417,777 kg) and offer 43,000 cubic feet of living and working space.
International contributions to the project will include European and Japanese laboratory modules and a Canadian robotic arm to assist with the construction and maintenance of the complex.

President Reagan ordered the construction of the space station in 1984, but after years of delays, redesigns and budget cuts the project remained on the drawing board. Russia, with its extensive space station experience, joined the effort in 1993 but has found it difficult to meet its financial commitments to the project.
